b: Definition: extracellular deposition of abnormal, insoluble misfolded protein fibrils (beta-pleated sheet structure)
Types: AL (light chain — associated with plasma cell disorders/myeloma), AA (serum amyloid A — associated with chronic inflammation/infection), transthyretin-related (familial/senile)
Diagnosis: Congo red stain — shows apple-green birefringence under polarised light
Organs affected: kidney (nephrotic syndrome), heart (restrictive cardiomyopathy), liver, spleen, nerves
Clinical relevance: chronic infections (TB, osteomyelitis) and inflammatory conditions (rheumatoid arthritis) predispose to AA amyloidosis

qs.q: A patient is diagnosed with cardiac amyloidosis causing restrictive cardiomyopathy. Which characteristic echocardiographic or structural feature is most classically associated with this specific form of restrictive cardiomyopathy?
o: Massive atrial dilation with normal walls
qs.e: Restrictive cardiomyopathy characteristically presents with normal ventricular wall thickness or slight thickening, normal chamber sizes, and massively dilated atria due to blood backing up. Amyloidosis is the most common cause overall.

qs.q: A renal biopsy specimen is evaluated for suspected fibrillary glomerulonephritis versus amyloidosis. Which specific feature distinguishes fibrillary GN from amyloid deposits?
o: Fibrillary GN deposits do not stain with Congo red
Fibrillary GN shows approximately 10 nm wide fibrils
Amyloid deposits contain diagnostic DNAJB9 markers
Amyloid fibrils are characteristically larger at 20 nm
qs.e: Fibrillary glomerulonephritis deposits do not stain with Congo red, whereas amyloid deposits do. Furthermore, fibrillary GN fibrils are larger (~20 nm) compared to amyloid fibrils (~10 nm).

qs.q: A pathologist identifies a specific co-chaperone for heat shock protein 70 within glomerular deposits as a sensitive and specific diagnostic marker for a rare glomerular disease that mimics amyloidosis. What is this marker protein?
qs.e: DNAJB9 has been identified as a highly sensitive and specific marker for fibrillary glomerulonephritis, found within its characteristic Congo red-negative deposits. Podocin and alpha-actinin 4 are structural podocyte proteins mutated in inherited forms of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Amyloidosis is the extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils that disrupt organ function. It can be primary (AL), secondary (AA) or hereditary (ATTR). Clinical thinking focuses on identifying the underlying cause, organ involvement and appropriate treatment.

sections.p: Amyloidosis is the accumulation of insoluble beta‑pleated sheet protein fibrils in tissues. The gold‑standard test is Congo red staining, which shows apple‑green birefringence under polarized light. Other supportive tests include serum free light chains, immunofixation, and organ‑specific imaging.

t.b: Detects excess kappa or lambda light chains; a high ratio suggests AL amyloidosis.
Identifies monoclonal protein; confirms plasma cell dyscrasia.
Shows free light chains in urine; supports AL diagnosis.
Elevated in chronic inflammation; indicates AA amyloidosis.
Assesses restrictive cardiomyopathy; helps stage cardiac involvement.
Confirms amyloid in kidney; guides treatment of nephrotic syndrome.

sections.p: Staging is organ‑specific. Cardiac staging uses troponin and NT‑proBNP; renal staging uses proteinuria and eGFR; hepatic staging uses bilirubin and transaminases. Higher stages predict poorer survival.
b: Cardiac stage I: normal troponin, low NT‑proBNP
Cardiac stage II: elevated troponin or NT‑proBNP

t.b: Elevated indicates myocardial injury; correlates with cardiac amyloid load.
High levels reflect ventricular wall stress; prognostic for heart failure.

sections.p: The most common causes differ by region. In low‑resource settings, chronic infections (TB, osteomyelitis) and inflammatory diseases (rheumatoid arthritis) drive AA amyloidosis. In high‑income areas, plasma cell disorders cause AL amyloidosis. Hereditary ATTR is less common but should be considered in familial cases.

t.b: Chronic immune activation can raise serum amyloid A; monitor for AA amyloidosis.
Recurrent infection may elevate SAA; consider in endemic areas.
Chronic hemolysis can increase SAA; watch for renal amyloid.

sections.p: Symptoms depend on organ involvement. Renal amyloid presents with proteinuria and edema; cardiac amyloid causes dyspnea, orthopnea, and arrhythmias; neuropathy manifests as numbness and weakness; hepatomegaly may be silent or cause abdominal discomfort.

t.b: Suggests nephrotic syndrome; check proteinuria.

sections.p: A systematic work‑up starts with basic labs, then organ‑specific imaging and biopsy. When advanced tests are unavailable, clinical judgment and simple tests guide management.

sections.p: Rapidly progressive renal failure, severe heart failure, unexplained weight loss, or recurrent infections are red flags. Complications include nephrotic syndrome, arrhythmias, and organ failure.
